job: Fresh graduate in computing and engineering
name: Pedro Bauer

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal day right now.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live at home above my dad's garage, where he fixes cars and sells tyres. I'm in the workshop most mornings, doing oil changes and brakes, then I apply for jobs in the afternoon and ask my old project supervisor for contacts. I share a room with my brother Tomas, who's sixteen and plays loud music.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What was the last stretch of study like, and what are you hoping for next?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I studied mechanical engineering and passed with an average mark. My final project was a test rig measuring gearbox efficiency, built in the workshop with a lecturer. I had no internship, since the firms wanted people who'd already done one, and so far about 60 applications to manufacturers have brought two rejections and a lot of silence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's about what I thought. At work I'd say the new tools are okay for quotes and paperwork. To friends I'd say I don't see the point of getting excited either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, nothing changes for me. Manufacturers hire fewer juniors than they did, and a pass degree without placements puts me at the back. I'm also in my dad's garage because I can't pay rent elsewhere, and I know he'd prefer I used my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, aim at smaller manufacturers within an hour's drive and ask my supervisor to introduce me to firms that make test equipment. I'd keep working in the garage and take a CAD certificate course for about 150 pounds. I'd also set aside 80 a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Stuck. Not scared, not happy, just waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the tools are okay for paperwork. Do you use them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now and then. I let an AI tool tidy up my emails and sometimes help with a CAD macro. I check everything, because I've seen it get a unit wrong.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your dad say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He says there's always a place for me in the garage. He means it kindly, but it makes me feel like I'm wasting four years.

I don't see the point of getting excited either way, so I stay **neutral**.
think: Manufacturers hire fewer **juniors**, and a pass degree without placements puts me at the back.
I'm in my dad's garage because I can't afford **rent** elsewhere.
do: Keep applying to small **manufacturers** within an hour's drive.
Ask my supervisor to introduce me to firms that make **test equipment**.
Take a **CAD certificate** course for about 150 pounds and save 80 a month.
feel: **Stuck**: not scared, not happy, just waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we'll adapt. Software will do a lot of the calculating and drafting in design offices. I'd tell my friends to learn the tools now, and I'd say machines on the shop floor are another story.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it makes my own route harder. The junior design and drafting work is the type that goes to software first, and that's the work a graduate would start with. The hands-on parts, like testing rigs and maintenance, stay with people for longer, and I'm more at home there anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use AI deliberately for CAD, simulation set-ups and reports, and I'd show those on a portfolio. I'd look hard at testing, maintenance and technician roles, where my garage experience counts. I'd also ask Dad whether we can add electric car servicing, which would need training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, more than frightened. I can see where it's going, I'm just late to it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your garage experience help you with a manufacturer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know how things fail. Most graduates have never taken a gearbox apart. In an interview I'd say I can read a drawing and fix the part.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a risk you're underselling the design side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably. I like the hands-on side, but if the jobs are mostly there, I'd rather follow them than the degree title.

steps.text: Use AI to build CAD and simulation examples for a portfolio

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no way anyone is ready. Two years is about the time it takes me to finish a project plan. I'd say the government should start paying for retraining, and I'd say it plainly at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be rattled. If AI does the thinking side of engineering better than I can, then the design offices don't need a graduate. I'd still have the garage, and robots for hands-on work are three years behind, which gives me a gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd shift entirely to the practical side: more garage work, a hands-on trade qualification, maybe an apprenticeship in vehicle electronics. I'd cut spending to rent-free basics, since I'm at home, and save 200 a month. I'd also have a conversation with Dad about whether the garage can carry the two of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shaky. I'd keep a straight face and not sleep much.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the garage carrying you. What does that mean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dad's takings are up and down. If I join full time, it's another wage the business has to find. I'd want it to be a real plan, not a favour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your brother Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomas not to choose a desk-only course. Pick something where you can use your hands. I'd say it's what I wish I'd thought of when I was his age.

say: Nobody is ready, since two years is about how long a **project plan** takes me.
The government should start paying for **retraining** now.
think: If AI does the thinking side of engineering better, design offices don't need a **graduate**.
Robots for hands-on work are three years behind, which gives me a **gap**.
do: Shift to the **practical** side with more garage work and a vehicle electronics apprenticeship.
Cut spending to basics and save **200 a month**.
Talk to Dad about whether the **garage** can carry two wages.
feel: **Shaky**; I'd keep a straight face and not sleep much.
S2.quote: I'd tell Tomas not to choose a desk-only course. Pick something where you can use your hands.
fieldNote: Turns toward **hands-on** work early because of the three-year robot lag.
Cautious about his **father's** takings and wants a real plan, not a favour.
Thinks of his younger **brother** and shares what he'd say.

steps.text: Apply for a vehicle electronics apprenticeship
Work full time in the family garage with a business plan
Cut spending to basics and save 200 a month
Talk with his dad about the garage supporting two wages

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a fair warning. I'd say employers should say what they plan to automate, and colleges should adjust courses. I'd mention it at a local business meeting and see what people think.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I'd be anxious but in a workable way. Get a first job quickly, learn on the job, and by 2031 I'd be someone who can fix machines and understand the software. Five years is enough to make myself useful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for a technician job at a manufacturer, even below my degree, and study part time for a mechatronics qualification. I'd save 150 a month and sit down with Dad about a share in the garage as it adds electric vehicle repair. I'd learn AI tools for diagnostics, since garages use them too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alert, not scared. Five years sounds like a plan with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why mechatronics?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's mechanics, electronics and software together, the stuff that's hard to replace. A machine that mixes all three still needs someone who knows how it all fits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the technician job doesn't come?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the garage is my fallback and my training ground. I'd rather have my own hands on something than be waiting.

say: Five years is a fair warning, so employers should say what they plan to **automate**.
Colleges should adjust their **courses** to match.
think: I'd be anxious but in a **workable** way.
By 2031 I could fix machines and understand the **software**, which makes me useful.

feel: **Alert**, not scared; five years sounds like a plan with a deadline.
S3.quote: I'd rather have my own hands on something than be waiting.

steps.text: Apply for technician jobs at manufacturers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time if people don't wait. I'd say schools should teach practical and digital skills together, and employers should pay for apprenticeships.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quietly, I'd say it's okay. A decade is enough to get settled in a job, move out and maybe start a family. I'd still worry about the dip when I'm established and the work changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep applying, take the first reasonable job and stay flexible. I'd save for a flat deposit, finish a mechatronics course and help Dad bring in electric car work. I'd try one new tool each year, so I'm not caught out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit easier. I'd treat it like a long project, and I'm good with projects.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'd get comfortable and miss the turn. If the plan is ten years, the danger is doing nothing for eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your dad think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say don't get ahead of yourself, take the job and see. He's seen trends come and go in car repair, so he's calm about it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one. I'd have no experience, no deposit and a degree that nobody asks about. What would help is apprenticeships with pay, honest forecasts and employers taking a chance on graduates who've got a bit of garage grease on their hands.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that I'd like people to see practical graduates as an asset. We can make things and fix them. I just need one place that says come on in.

headlineQuote: We can make things and fix them. I just need one place that says come on in.
portrait: Pedro is a 23-year-old **mechanical engineering** graduate with a pass, no internship and about 60 applications sent.
He lives above his father's **garage**, works there mornings and shares a room with his brother Tomas.
He is centre in his views, uses AI sometimes, and changes his plans once a thing is **proven**.
His mood is **anxious** in most worlds, alarmed at two years and uneasy when he has a decade.
He leans on hands-on skills, **mechatronics** study and the family garage as his hedge.
biggestWorry: The **2028** case, with no experience, no deposit and a degree nobody asks about.
whatWouldHelp: Paid **apprenticeships**, honest forecasts and employers who take a chance on practical graduates.
